title: The poem, its title and Gibb's text
greek: Arabic kun fa-yakūn ('Be! and it is'); Turkish kün-fe-kân
short: Ghazel [7] in Gibb's History of Ottoman Poetry (1900): God speaks through Yunus, opening with the Qur'anic creative command 'Be! and it is'.
body: Gibb printed this as the second of 'two of Yunus's pantheistic ghazels', straight after 'Faith, idol, Ka'ba-fane am I' (also in the archive). His note explains that 'Be! and it is', God's word of command and its instant effect, sums up the divine creative power and recurs throughout the Qur'an (he cites Q 2:117; it also appears at 3:47, 16:40 and 36:82); he compares Psalm 33:9, 'he spake, and it was done'. The speaker who claims to be that 'Mighty One' is not Yunus as a private man: as in the preceding ghazel, the claim is that God's own voice sounds through the dervish. Gibb's footnote on the Light verse (Q 24:35) belongs to that earlier poem's 'What coalless burns', not to this one. Yunus (c. 1240-1320) wrote in plain Anatolian Turkish; Gibb translated from the lithographed Divan of 1884-5.

title: The refrain 'am I' and the internal rhymes
greek: Arabic radīf ('one who rides behind'), Turkish redif
short: Every couplet ends on 'am I', Gibb's rendering of a repeated end-word (redif), and most first lines carry a chiming internal rhyme.
body: Gibb's preface says his translations try to reproduce the outer form of the original: its rhyme pattern, the syllable count where possible, and the movement of the accent. Here that means a fixed refrain, 'am I', closing every couplet, as the redif closes every couplet of a ghazel. The first line of each couplet has its own internal chime (seed / proceed, be / iniquity, freeze / bestows / businesses, sooth / Truth, create / rotate). Gibb notes that most of Yunus's ghazels use the favourite Turkish device of a thrice-repeated internal sub-rhyme, close to what learned poets called musammat verse, and that his rhymes are often loose or merely assonant. The relentless refrain turns the poem into a litany: each new divine work is claimed with the same two words, so that the whole of creation is gathered into one 'I'.

title: 'ere 'tis cut': daily bread
short: Gibb explains: God assigns each creature its daily portion while the grain is still growing, before it is reaped.
body: Gibb's note glosses the line as the One 'who while the grain is yet growing assigns to each creature its daily portion'. The idea is the Qur'anic doctrine of rizq, God's provision: 'there is no creature on the earth but its sustenance depends on God' (Q 11:6). The portion is fixed before the harvest, indeed before the creature asks; Turkish piety still speaks of each person's appointed rızk. 'King' (Arabic malik, one of the divine Names) sets the image in a royal household, where a ruler feeds his dependants. The same theme of unequal distribution returns in couplet 4 ('lacks a groat').

title: Man from seed, bird from egg
short: Qur'anic signs of creation: man made from a drop of fluid, the living bird brought out of the egg.
body: The Qur'an repeatedly names the making of man 'from a drop' (nutfa) as a sign of God's power (e.g. Q 16:4, 76:2), and speaks of God bringing the living out of the dead (Q 6:95), which commentators illustrate by the chick from the egg. Gibb singles out this very formula when he describes Yunus's thought: the poet 'openly proclaims that he is God' who creates man from seed and brings the bird from the egg, and Gibb adds that Yunus's pantheism is frank, not hidden behind allegory as in later poets. The couplet thus chooses the humblest everyday wonders, birth and hatching, as proof of the one creative will.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (London: Luzac, 1900), ch. on Yunus Emre, pp. 166-73, with Gibb's notes

title: 'the Tongue of Power'
short: God's own speech, which makes the poet speak: the same phrase closes the previous ghazel, 'It is not Yunus sayeth this'.
body: 'Power' here is the divine omnipotence (Arabic qudra, Turkish kudret). In the ghazel that Gibb prints just before this one ('Faith, idol, Ka'ba-fane am I'), the last couplet explains that it is not Yunus who speaks but 'Power's Tongue'. In this poem the speaker is the one 'who makes the Tongue of Power to speak': the voice is God's, Yunus is only its instrument. This is the usual defence of ecstatic Sufi utterance (shath): the 'I' of such lines belongs to God, not to the mystic's self, which has been annihilated (fanā'). Schimmel describes how such utterances, from al-Hallaj onward, were both admired and condemned. Compare couplet 10, 'Who giveth me this tongue is He'.

title: 'He who remembereth aye'
short: Gibb cites Qur'an 2:152, 'Remember me, and I will remember you': God remembers those who remember Him.
body: Gibb's note points to the Qur'anic promise 'Remember me, and I will remember you; thank me, and be not ungrateful' (Q 2:152; Gibb, using an older numbering, gives ii, 147). The verse underlies the Sufi practice of dhikr (Turkish zikir), the rhythmic repetition of God's Name in the dervish lodges where Yunus's poems were sung as hymns (ilahi). The speaker claims to be the remembering God, so the human practice of remembrance is answered from the divine side. 'Aye' is the archaic adverb 'always', one of Gibb's many deliberate archaisms.

title: Ascetics and sinners: predestination
short: God makes some men ascetics and others sinners: a bold statement of predestination that Yunus takes up again in the mesnevi Gibb prints next.
body: The 'ascetic' (Turkish zâhid) is the man of outward piety; in Persian and Turkish mystical poetry he is often a mild butt, contrasted with the lover. Here both piety and 'iniquity' are attributed to God's will, a statement of the doctrine of the divine decree (qadar). The theological difficulty is real, and Yunus did not avoid it: in the passage Gibb prints straight after the next ghazel, a mesnevi beginning 'O my God, if so be Thou should question me', the poet asks God why He created him so faulty and says that whatever he has done, God has done. Gibb introduces it as an attack on the crude ideas of God held by the ignorant or fanatical orthodox. Readers differ on whether such lines express fatalism or the mystic's sense that nothing exists apart from God.

title: 'Argument and Proof' who veils faults
short: God as the decisive proof of Himself, who also covers His servants' sins: probably the divine epithet Settâr, 'the Veiler'.
body: 'Argument and Proof' most likely renders the Arabic pair hujja and burhan, terms of theology meaning the conclusive evidence that establishes a truth; the Qur'an calls its message a 'proof (burhan) from your Lord' (Q 4:174). Gibb gives no note, so the exact Turkish words cannot be checked from this text. The second half of the line, the one 'who veils their faults and flaws', recalls the popular divine epithet Settâr (Arabic sattār), He who covers sins rather than exposing them; the theme is common in Turkish devotional language. Set beside the first half of the couplet, the line suggests that the God who decrees the sinner's sin also hides it in mercy.

title: 'lacks a groat'
short: A groat was an old English silver coin worth four pence: one man is given horses, wives and children, another lacks even a penny.
body: The groat (OED) was an English silver coin worth four pence, first issued in 1279 and struck regularly until the later seventeenth century, and proverbial for a trifling sum; Gibb prints no Turkish text, but his 'groat' evidently stands for some small coin of the original. The couplet returns to the theme of rizq (couplet 1): wealth and poverty, horses and family, are all apportioned by God. The tone is not social protest but acceptance; the same 'One of gracious sway' gives to one and withholds from another. Gibb's archaic diction ('doth', 'groat', 'the while') is meant to give a Victorian reader a sense of the age and rusticity of Yunus's Turkish, which Gibb calls the most rugged of any Turkish poet.

anchor: the Soul of souls in fay
title: 'the Soul of souls in fay'
greek: Persian jān-i jān, Turkish cân-ı cân ('soul of the soul'); fay < Old French fei ('faith')
short: God as the life within all lives; 'in fay' is Gibb's archaic tag 'in faith', i.e. 'truly'.
body: 'Soul of souls' is a standard Persian and Turkish mystical title for God or the Beloved (jān-i jān, cân-ı cân): the life that animates every living thing. The couplet has just listed snow, frost and the feeding of every beast, so the phrase sums up the catalogue: all these 'businesses' are the work of one indwelling life. 'In fay' is the archaic English oath 'in faith', 'truly' (OED, fay, from Old French fei), used chiefly for the rhyme with 'am I'; Gibb fills out several lines with such tags ('in sooth', 'yea', 'aye'), which is the price of his strict rhyming.

title: 'Eternity' and 'the Unconditioned Truth'
greek: Arabic al-Ḥaqq ('the Real, the Truth'); muṭlaq ('absolute, unconditioned')
short: 'The Truth' (al-Haqq) is the Sufis' preferred name for God; 'unconditioned' renders the idea of absolute Being, limited by nothing.
body: Al-Haqq, 'the Real' or 'the Truth', is one of the Names of God and the favourite name for Him in Sufi writing; in Turkish it is simply Hak. Its most famous use is the cry attributed to the mystic al-Hallaj, executed in Baghdad in 922: 'Ana'l-Haqq', 'I am the Truth'. Gibb notes that Yunus elsewhere says he was Mansur (al-Hallaj) and also Mansur's executioners. 'Unconditioned' renders the philosophical notion of the absolute (mutlak), Being without any limit or attribute; 'Eternity' points to God as without beginning (ezel) and without end (ebed). On Yunus's own lips such claims are, in Sufi terms, the speech of the annihilated self.

title: Khizr and the Water of Life
greek: Arabic al-Khiḍr ('the Green One'), Turkish Hızır
short: The immortal guide of Islamic legend, guardian of the Water of Life; Yunus says even Khizr's sins are forgiven by the One who speaks.
body: Gibb's long note calls Khizr 'a very vague personage' met everywhere in Oriental poetry: identified with the unnamed servant of God whom Moses follows in Qur'an 18:60-82, sometimes confused with Elijah and St George, guardian of the Stream of Life, which he alone found and drank in the Alexander legend, and so immortal. He appears to the pious in distress as an old man and vanishes when recognised. The name is linked to greenness (perhaps, Gibb suggests, evergreen and so immortal). In Turkey he is Hızır, celebrated with Ilyas at the spring festival of Hıdrellez. Gibb reads the line as saying that the Water of Life Khizr may offer 'to-morrow' is nothing to the speaker, who is the one who forgives Khizr his sins.

title: The Four Things and the Sign
greek: Arabic ʿanāṣir-i arbaʿa ('the four elements'); āya ('sign')
short: The four elements of ancient and Islamic natural philosophy, fire, air, earth and water; the speaker is the 'Sign' behind them all.
body: The 'Four Things' are named in the next line: Fire, Air, Earth and Water, the four elements of Greek natural philosophy (Empedocles, Aristotle) taken over by Islamic science, from which all bodies are compounded. Gibb's opening chapters on the Ottoman picture of the cosmos explain this system. 'Sign' renders the Qur'anic aya: everything in creation is a sign pointing to its Maker ('We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves', Q 41:53), and the same word means a verse of the Qur'an. The speaker claims to be not one sign among many but 'the Sign indeed', the meaning that all the elements spell out.

title: The veils of flesh
short: The body and its parts are veils that both hide and reveal the God within; He is 'the Hid and Open'.
body: In Sufi thought the created world, and the body above all, is a veil (hijab) between the soul and God; a well-known tradition speaks of God's veils of light and darkness. Here the veils of flesh, skin, bone, life and body are not obstacles set up by an enemy but garments the One Himself 'holds'. The second line answers the image with a Qur'anic pair: God is knower of 'the unseen and the seen' (al-ghayb wa'sh-shahada, Q 59:22), so He is at once 'the Hid and Open'. The same body that hides Him is one of the places where He appears, the idea modern Turkish scholars call tecelli, manifestation.

anchor: The Outer and the Inner I
title: Outer and Inner, Former and Latter
short: Four divine Names from Qur'an 57:3: 'He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward'.
body: The line translates almost word for word Qur'an 57:3, 'He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, and He knows all things'. The four Names (al-Awwal, al-Akhir, al-Zahir, al-Batin) were a favourite text of the Sufis, for whom they showed that nothing lies outside God in time or in being. The pair 'Outer and Inner' (zahir and batin) also names the two levels of religion, the outward law and the inward truth, a distinction central to Anatolian dervish piety. Gibb's 'Former and Latter' keeps the rhyme on 'I' but blurs the plainer 'First and Last'.

title: 'I am He, and He is I'
greek: Arabic waḥdat al-wujūd ('unity of being'); ittiḥād ('union')
short: The poem's boldest line, the identity of the mystic and God; scholars differ over whether to call it pantheism.
body: Gibb called this poem pantheistic and praised Yunus's frankness: unlike later poets, he does not hide the doctrine of the ultimate Unity behind allegory, and Gibb traced it to the lyric Divan of Jalal al-Din Rumi. Orthodox critics of Sufism condemned claims of union (ittihad) as heresy, the charge on which al-Hallaj died. Many modern scholars avoid the word 'pantheism', a European term: Tatcı describes Yunus's outlook as tevhid, in which being is one, the Absolute Being is God, and created things are manifestations (tecelli) of His Names and attributes; Schimmel similarly warns against reading Sufi 'unity of being' as simple identity of God and world. On that reading the 'I' that says 'I am He' is the self that has passed away in God. The refrain lets both readings stand.

title: 'truchman'
short: An interpreter or go-between: between God and the mystic there is no intermediary, no translator.
body: 'Truchman' (OED) is an archaic English word for an interpreter, borrowed through medieval Latin and French from Arabic tarjuman, the same word that gives Turkish tercüman and English 'dragoman'. Gibb's choice is pointed: a word of the Levant trade, used of the interpreters at Ottoman courts, now denies that any interpreter is needed. Between the mystic and God nothing stands, neither priest nor scholar nor book, because 'all wroughten there' (all that is made) is plain to the speaker. The line also comments on the poem itself: the tongue that speaks is God's gift, so the poet is no translator of the divine word but its direct voice. 'Wroughten' is a pseudo-archaic participle of 'work'.

anchor: yon Sea that rolls each way
title: The Sea that rolls each way
greek: Persian daryā, Turkish deniz ('sea'); Arabic baḥr
short: The ocean of Being, a stock Sufi image: creatures are its waves or drops, and the One is the whole sea.
body: The sea is among the commonest images of Sufi poetry for the one divine Being: individual things are its waves, foam or drops, which rise, take shape and fall back without ever ceasing to be water. Yunus uses the image often in his Turkish poems, and Rumi, whom Gibb names as his master in thought, uses it constantly. 'That rolls each way' suggests a sea with no shore and no single current, moving in all directions at once: infinite, and present everywhere. Placed after 'Who giveth me this tongue is He', the image hints that the poem's own words are waves of that sea.

title: Throne and Stool ('Arsh and Kursi)
short: The Throne and the Footstool of God in the Qur'an; Gibb suggests that as they 'rotate' they stand for the ninth and eighth heavenly spheres.
body: Gibb's note gives the original words, 'Arsh and Kursi. The Qur'an speaks of God settling on the Throne ('arsh, e.g. Q 7:54), and the Throne verse says His Kursi, chair or footstool, 'extends over the heavens and the earth' (Q 2:255). In Islamic cosmology they lie above the seven heavens. Because Yunus speaks of them as rotating, Gibb suggests that the poet means them as the Ninth and Eighth Spheres, the outermost heavens of the Ptolemaic system, which turn the rest; he explains the system in his opening chapters. The couplet thus completes the poem's cosmic sweep, from grain and snow to the outer heavens.

title: The thousand and one Names
greek: Arabic al-asmāʾ al-ḥusnā ('the most beautiful Names')
short: God's Names: the usual count is ninety-nine, but Gibb notes that some say there are a thousand and one.
body: The Qur'an says 'to God belong the most beautiful Names' (Q 7:180), and a well-known hadith counts ninety-nine of them; the litany of the Names is recited on prayer beads. Gibb's note records that some authorities count a thousand and one, the figure Yunus uses and a popular one in Turkish devotion (bin bir ad). Many of the poem's titles are among them: King (al-Malik), the Truth (al-Haqq), the First and Last, the Outer and Inner. In Sufi thought every created thing reflects one or more Names, which is why the speaker who claims all things can also claim all the Names.

title: The signature: 'Yunus, He of the Koran'
short: The poet names himself in the last couplet, as ghazel convention requires, and identifies himself with the Author of the Qur'an.
body: By convention the last couplet of a ghazel (the makta) contains the poet's pen name (mahlas); Yunus usually signs simply 'Yunus'. Gibb's note explains 'He of the Koran' as 'the Author of the Koran, i.e. God'. Read straight, the line makes the boldest claim in the poem: Yunus is God. Read against the previous ghazel's ending, 'It is not Yunus sayeth this, 'tis Power's Tongue', it can mean the reverse: what speaks under the name Yunus is God's word, and the human Yunus has vanished. Gibb also notes in his chapter that the received Divan, lithographed in 1884-5, can hardly be exactly what Yunus wrote, and modern editors warn that other poets, notably Âşık Yunus of Bursa, also signed 'Yunus'.
